# What 271,000 mortgage decisions taught me about building a fair approval model

**Sabeeh Ansari · LoanWise AI · case study** — every number below is regenerated by `python -m ml.run` (about 4 minutes) into [`reports/ml/REPORT.md`](../reports/ml/REPORT.md).

## The problem with version 1

LoanWise v1 was a working product: a React and FastAPI app that scores an application, explains it with SHAP, audits fairness and has an LLM write the decision letter. The ML underneath was weak, though. It used 614 rows from a Kaggle dataset, credit history was a yes/no flag, and the currency was unclear. The fairness audit rested on **112 women**. Honest evaluation showed the model barely beat a one-line rule. The engineering was ahead of the evidence, so for v2 I replaced the data instead of tuning the model.

## Data and setup

- **Source:** public **HMDA** records, which US lenders must file for every mortgage application. I used Georgia home-purchase decisions.
- **Split:** trained on **2022** (151,421 applications) and tested once on **2023** (120,170). A time-based split is the honest test for a model that will meet next year's applicants.
- **Size:** 72,998 women and 63,391 Black applicants. The fairness audit now has statistical power.
- **Reproducibility:** downloads are pinned with SHA-256 checksums. Every scoping rule (e.g. first-lien, owner-occupied, site-built) logs how many rows it removed. The pipeline is a tested Python package (34 unit tests), not a notebook.

## Finding 1: two leaks, one obvious and one subtle

HMDA rows contain fields that only exist **after** the lender decides: the interest rate, closing costs and denial reasons. A model given them scores **ROC-AUC 1.000**, which is meaningless. A missingness audit flags them automatically; `interest_rate`, for example, is blank for 100% of denials.

The second leak looked innocent. `preapproval` is known before any decision, yet **all 8,613 applications that requested one were approved**. Denied preapprovals are filed under a different action code, which my approve/deny query excluded. The missingness audit could not see this because nothing was blank. A **separation audit** caught it: it flags any category where only one outcome ever occurs. The leak had inflated ROC-AUC (0.799 → 0.789 once removed). It had also made automation look **13× more viable** than it is: 11.8% vs 0.9% of applications at a 2% error budget.

## Finding 2: the model is useful, with a ceiling

| Model (tested on 2023) | ROC-AUC | Denial PR-AUC |
|---|---|---|
| Approve if DTI ≤ 43% (the textbook rule) | 0.614 | 0.139 |
| Logistic regression | 0.725 | 0.405 |
| **XGBoost, monotonic (chosen)** | **0.789** | **0.537** |
| XGBoost, unconstrained | 0.798 | 0.555 |

I chose the **monotonic** model and gave up 0.009 AUC for a guarantee the unconstrained model lacks: more debt, more leverage or less income can never *raise* approval. It is also well calibrated (expected calibration error **0.003**). Its top factor, debt-to-income, matches the lenders' own most common denial reason (39% of denials).

The model never denies anyone. It **auto-approves or refers to a person**. Allowing at most 5% of auto-approvals to be ones the lender denied, it automates **71.5%** of applications and sends 67% of lender denials to a human. A tighter 2% budget automates almost nothing. HMDA has no credit scores, and credit history and incomplete applications together account for 24% of denials, so the public data cannot support a stricter policy.

## Finding 3: "fairer on average" is not fair at the threshold

From financial features alone, the model reproduces about two-thirds of the lenders' Black–White approval gap: **−6.2 points vs −9.8**. The rest is not explained by the variables available here. That is not proof of discrimination, because credit scores are missing. But averages hide the decision. At the 5% operating threshold, **Black applicants whom the lender approved were 20.6 points more likely to be referred for manual review** instead of auto-approved. A small shift in average scores becomes a large one at a cut-off.

Two interventions, measured rather than assumed:

| Change | Black referral gap | ROC-AUC |
|---|---|---|
| Base model | +20.6 pp | 0.789 |
| Add census-tract features | **+28.5 pp** (geography is a proxy for race) | 0.795 |
| Reweigh training data by race × outcome | **+17.3 pp** | 0.786 |

So the shipped design excludes geography and treats referral as review, not denial. It also reports group gaps at the operating threshold, not only on average, because that is where harm happens.

## What I would do next

Add credit-score proxies or a second state to test whether the ceiling and the threshold effect generalise. Then evaluate threshold policies that bound the referral gap directly, and wire the v2 model into the app with these checks as release gates in CI.
